utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. I've heard that there are possibly some oral submissions by a party. Is that the case? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, everyone, Your Honours. Yeah, that was the plan, and I can think -- as you know, that we've been trying to fill this week with witnesses, since we had the additional Monday a few weeks back, and as the Court knows, Mr. Thayer sent an e-mail about our intention to try to call Mr. Blaszczyk about the Mladic diaries. And we have, of course, the e-mail from the Court, with your concerns on that point. And we've been speaking, as we always do, with the Defence about that -- about this week and about Mr. Blaszczyk's potential testimony on this topic. And Mr. Gajic and I spoke a few days ago, after he had a chance to consult with his client, and he will have something to say on this as well. But it was our agreement, as I understand, that we would speak to you orally on this topic. Mr. Gajic has explained that it is the position of the general to take no position on this issue, and so we -- it looks like we are in a potential gap situation. So I would offer an oral motion at this time to amend Mr. Blaszczyk's summary to include testifying about how the Prosecutor got the Mladic diaries, and some of the documents related to that seizure, and some of the documents related to the authenticity of it. It's pretty much what he testified to back in July in the Karadzic case. It was short testimony. The Defence was provided with all that material, I think, about a week or two after he testified in July, so they've had all this material, they know what this is about, the diaries, Mr. Blaszczyk's testimony. So just to assure you that there is nothing new, no surprises here, and so we've been discussing with Mr. Gajic whether or not we might be able to take up that time by having Mr. Blaszczyk basically do what he did in the Mladic case. And, of course, we're prepared to file material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you're referring to the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, wishful thinking. The Karadzic case, excuse me. And so there are some of the materials associated with that testimony that don't have 65 ter numbers in our case because, as you know, these diaries came in at a point and we've been all gathering together this material to be able to do this properly for you, in terms of writing, so it was very clear. What is clear is that the Defence has the material, they are not taking a position on it, and what can be done is Mr. Blaszczyk can testify this week in direct, and if the general needs more time to prepare for cross, like we've done before, we can fit that in when the time is right for the Defence. And that way, we wouldn't -- hopefully, we wouldn't lose court time and this material could be dealt with in this way. Of course, it's just been a matter of trying to fill this gap, and so it's not perfect, but there's no surprises for anyone on this. And we've been working together, like we always do in these situations, and we appreciate the Court's concern about that. But as far as I know, we're ready to go. If we can get -- well, we want to, of course, hear from the general and Mr. Gajic, if they have any particular concerns, and I can answer any that we have, and perhaps we'll be able to get your approval to go ahead orally, as opposed to filing anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your position is understandable, but can you clarify? In fact, you are moving for the addition of Mr. Blaszczyk to the 65 ter witness list in respect to the diaries of Mr. Mladic, his summary, and some exhibits to include into the 65 ter exhibit list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's very well stated, Mr. President, especially since you're certainly the expert on these Rules. But that's correct, absolutely. And if -- I think that says it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, I think we are -- we have received the new summary, and I would like to know the concrete exhibits you want to use with the witness. I'm not aware of any submission in that respect with a list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's my understanding that that's being assembled, but it's the same group that he testified to. So it's a known quantity, and we just need to get it typed up - I know we're working on that - and see if there is any additional material that would be thrown in there. But it's fundamentally what was used before, and we will get that list for you very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You say it is well known. I'm quite sure that it is well known to the OTP and well known to the Defence, but the Chamber would like to know which exhibits you want to use with the witness. Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet all the parties present. I would like these proceedings to end as God wills it and not as I will it, and may God help us all. As far as what Mr. McCloskey has said, the Defence will in no way interfere with the way the Prosecution intends to proceed in this matter, and we're quite happy for the Trial Chamber to make its decision on this matter that has been presented by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the moment, there's no need for a decision. We are waiting for your list of exhibits to be used with Mr. Blaszczyk in the continuation of his testimony. Now we should start with the next witness, if there is nothing else to raise. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. He is here. He does have protective measures, as we can all see, and we would request that he receive a caution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We turn into closed session for a moment so that the witness can enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the witness please rise. Please wait a short moment. First of all, good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. My apologies for the delay. We had to discuss some procedural matters, but now it is time to examine you. Before we start with that: On the request of the Prosecution, I would like to give you some guidance about your testimony. In our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 90(E), there is a provision which should protect you if there are any problems. And I would like to quote from these Rules, and I hope you understand that. I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Sir, did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, for the Prosecution, has some questions for you, I suppose. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All right. And we're up-loading the pseudonym sheet, so we'll have that in a moment and make sure we get the name correctly, but we won't mention it at this point. Perhaps we should go into -- well, first, I can ask you some basics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember testifying in the Popovic case back in March of 2007 in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked then, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I would, on that account, Mr. President, offer the transcripts P1350 and P1351 into evidence, along with the associated exhibits, 1352 through 1357, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, we should have, for the record, the name - not the full name but the pseudonym - of the witness on the screen so we know who is sitting here as a witness. Sir, I have to tell you the protective measures granted for you in the previous case are still in place. That means everybody in the courtroom will only refer to you by a pseudonym instead of a name, and your face will not be visible on the internet and in the courtroom, so that you are fully protected. Mr. McCloskey, which is the number of the pseudonym sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that has just popped up on e-court now. So it's 65 ter 6797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem is it is not on the exhibit list for this witness, but I'm sure we will have it on the screen very soon. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, is that your name? Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now that we've got that established, I think I should now formally offer the exhibits P1350 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps first this sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. This sheet, I would offer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1368. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, it's under seal, as Ms. Stewart reminds me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Under seal, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then P1350 through 1357, the transcripts and exhibits that came into evidence through this witness in his prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Witness, you also testified in the Perisic case not long ago, is that correct, on similar subject matter?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I will now read a short summary of your testimony to get us started. And we need to start off with the first two paragraphs in private session, Mr. President, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, the exhibits, P1350, 1351, and 1352 through 1357, will be received as exhibits, some of them under seal. These are P1350 and P1353 through 1357. We turn now to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A few days after the fall of Srebrenica - the witness doesn't remember exactly how many - the witness was called to a meeting at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. The meeting took place in the office of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Vinko Pandurevic. There, the witness encountered a tall, well-built, grey-haired man of approximately 50 or 55 years of age. He was wearing a camouflage uniform and identified himself as Colonel Beara. After introducing himself, Colonel Beara delivered a brief speech, stating that they had a lot of prisoners at various locations in the Zvornik municipality and that they were having a very hard time controlling them. Colonel Beara explained that pursuant to the order of, in quotes, "two presidents," they had to, quote, "get rid of them," and that he expected the municipality to help take care of that. The witness testified that he understood that Colonel Beara wanted him to assist with the burial of the bodies of the Muslims by providing equipment, machinery, and access to municipal utility companies. Colonel Beara went on to tell the witness that the witness had to obey his orders as he was the commander at the barracks. The witness was surprised by Colonel Beara's speech. He did not respond to it or ask Colonel Beara any questions. The witness left Zvornik to go on holiday to the coast of Montenegro immediately after this meeting with Colonel Beara. While his vacation had been pre-planned, he hastened his departure in reaction to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, is that a correct account of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And today, in court, do you stand by that information that I just read out?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, in your own words, as you can remember them, what Beara said to you in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: He said that there were captured Muslim fighters at a number of locations throughout Zvornik, from Srebrenica, which they were finding difficult to control, and that they had to get rid of them. I was surprised, and probably judging by my reaction, he said that this was an order from two presidents and that he was the person in charge in the barracks now. I didn't say anything. The meeting was finished. I left Zvornik. I reported to the president of the Municipal Assembly that I was leaving Zvornik for 15 days or so, I got into my car and I left. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did Beara say about getting rid of them? What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes, he said that he expected help from the municipal authorities. I understood that to mean that, since we didn't have military units, that the civilian authorities could only help with the burial, not with the executions. What I understood was that it would be our part, our duty, to take part in these burials of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you have just mentioned executions and burials. Did you learn that information from Mr. -- Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: No, I didn't learn that then. Later, when I came back, everything was already over. Nobody talked about it openly, but everything was known about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have said that he expected you to assist in the burials of the Muslims; is that correct? Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: That was my conclusion. This is why I left the Zvornik municipality. I didn't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did he say that led you to believe that these people were going to need to be buried?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: He explained that the situation was alarming, that it was difficult to control the prisoners, that he had to get rid of them. Because it was wartime for three years and the technology was already familiar to us, that -- I mean, had he had to have taken them somewhere else, to another area, perhaps he would have expressed himself differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "technology," what kind of technology are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I meant -- I meant the choosing of words; terminology.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said "terminology" the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the way he termed things. I would have probably sought some transport assistance or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've testified numerous times that he asked you to bury them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes, to assist in the burial process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who were these people -- where were the people located that he wanted you to assist in burying?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: In a number of locations in the municipality of Zvornik, such as schools, cultural halls, et cetera. This is what I learned only later, because at that point in time I wasn't aware of those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did he mean when he told you to "get rid of" the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I don't know what he meant, but the way I understood it was that they had to be rid of, as it was done later on, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You need to explain that. I know this is difficult, but what did he mean by getting "rid of"?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I understood it to mean that they had to be executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the witness is being asked to put forth his opinion and to discuss the opinions of others. The witness was clear on what he concluded, and I don't know what the purpose is of this exercise that the witness should try to guess what this person meant and what he concluded based on that. He didn't conclude that based on the other person's opinion, he concluded what he did based on what was said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey got an answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Colonel Beara ever suggest that these people would be buried alive before execution?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I don't understand. How can people be buried alive, and by using what method?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned that he wanted them getting rid of and he wanted them buried, and you said you believed that meant they should be executed. I just wanted to make sure what he was telling you was that they would be executed before they would be buried or would they be killed by being buried alive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't use the words that they had to be killed, not literally. He basically said that they had to get rid of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, the Prosecutor, before the commencement of the proceedings today, asked of you to caution the witness, and now he wants the witness to say something that may incriminate him. I would kindly ask that the question be rephrased, because what somebody thought cannot be used as evidence either against me, or the witness, or any other participants in the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the beginning of the testimony of the witness, the witness was explained the meaning of Rule 90(E). I think this is absolutely sufficient, and Mr. -- and at the end of the trial, the Chamber will give weight to the answers, if this is evidence or not. It is up to the Chamber to decide on that at the end. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you remember testifying at the Popovic trial that you'd seen on television, I believe you said, someone that was coming to The Hague identified as a Mr. Beara, and you didn't think that was the same person that you had seen in that office that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But the description as you've testified in Popovic and as I've reiterated in the summary is the correct description; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see the rank insignia on the person that identified himself as Colonel Beara in that office?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what rank was it, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we now go to P00014, known to us as the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's note-book. And if we could go to English page 4, B/C/S page 131. And if need be, Witness, or Your Honours, I have the original of that note-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, do you remember being interviewed by the OTP, by a man named Julian Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was back on 7th of April, 2006, and do you remember him showing you this entry in the duty officer note-book where -- and this should not be broadcast. We best go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But this document should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did -- you asked them to turn off the tape-recorder, and they did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then you told them your experience with Colonel Beara in the office?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then did they turn the tape-recorder back on, to your knowledge, and ask you the same questions?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I don't think they asked the same questions. I think I provided the second part of my statement two days after that in the premises in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, did you finish up your statement on the -- with the tape-recorder going and tell them the story on the record, on the tape-recorder?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I think also for a period of time the tape-recorder was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But did you tell them about what Beara had told you at some point with the tape-recorder on?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I didn't -- I wasn't able to focus, and I wasn't able to perceive whether the tape-recorder was on or off. It seemed like the end of the world to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I thought that that period had gone and that 11 years later I wouldn't be asked about it, because everyone I knew had already been invited or called to provide statements or testified. I believed that I could escape that fate and that there were those who had much more knowledge about it. I still think that. I still think it could all have been done without me. It changed my life a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You just mentioned that there was more than just you and Colonel Beara at the office at the Zvornik Brigade. How many other people were in that room?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: That's the problem. I don't seem to be able to recall that at all. I remember Beara, but I don't know who was there as well to my side. I tried to recall, but I can't, and I wouldn't like to put some people into the situation I am now in without them actually having been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, just roughly, how many people were in that room besides you and Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: It was a small room, so four soldiers, I believe, and I don't know who was there on the side where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever, during this wartime period, seen General Tolimir in the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Only once, when there was a session of the Executive Council. I was there, as well as some of my associates and the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. Suddenly, General Mladic and General Gvero, as well as General Tolimir, came in. They greeted everyone but stayed there briefly only. They were probably looking for Mr. Pandurevic. That was the only time I saw Mr. Tolimir in person, whereas I saw him on numerous occasions on TV. I never spoke to him, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe what happened when, at this session of the Executive Council, Mladic, Tolimir and Gvero showed up? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: They came in, we got up to our feet, General Mladic asked Mr. Pandurevic what he was doing there, telling him that he was supposed to be with the army. It was partly in jest, but he may well have been serious. Mr. Pandurevic stood stock still and explained to him that he wanted the civilian authorities to know about what they could help the army with. It may have lasted for about five minutes, and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who left?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic -- General Mladic, General Gvero, General Tolimir, and Mr. Pandurevic. I think at the time he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just one last question, if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session. We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One question I forgot to ask you is: This time where Generals Mladic, Tolimir and Gvero came to your meeting in Zvornik, just roughly, when was that in relation to, you know, when Srebrenica fell in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think it was a month or more before all of that, before Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I have a question for you. I would like to get some clarification. On page 12, line 3 and 4, you said -- you were asked: "You have said that he expected you to assist in the burials of the Muslims; is that correct? Do you stand by that?" Your answer was:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was planning that holiday before, and my wife and friends were already on the Montenegrin coast. So it was just a matter of days when I would also leave, but this actually speeded things up. So I went that day, and I wish I had gone a day before, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, you have used the document P14, which is still on the screen before us. What about the last document on your list, P1358, MFI? It has the same title, "Zvornik Brigade Duty Officer Log-Book." Is that the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I had thought it was, but let me -- let me clarify. Mr. President, it was my understanding that this is the duty officer note-book. There's only one. It's a very important exhibit for this case. It's my understanding it's already into evidence. It came in through a 92 quater witness, and it should be P0014, but I believe it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is my understanding, too. That means we don't need it again as an exhibit with the number P1358 MFI, so that we can leave this number open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My understanding, this document can be crossed out on the list of the Registry from the 12th of November, 2010. It means we have it not with the number P1358.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's my understanding. Some of these sneak their way in in other ways that we're not always able to see very well. So I think that should clear it up. We might need to redact something. Yes, there's a -- it looks like page 22, lines 12, 13, 14, 15, 16. Line 16 is the troublesome one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because his position is mentioned there, we will redact that part of my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you start your cross-examination, we would like to know your time estimation for cross-examination of this witness. We haven't received that yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that I will need one hour, one hour and a half at the most. It depends on the answers of the witness. Then we'll have a break, I guess, and then the Prosecutor will have his redirect. I don't know what he will ask.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last thing that Mr. Tolimir said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please go ahead with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to greet the witness, and I'm going to put a number of questions to which you can answer or you cannot, perhaps not an answer, depending on your position in relation to the warning or the caution that the Judge mentioned at the beginning. Let's look at page 20 of today's transcript. When Mr. McCloskey asked you whether you had seen General Tolimir, and then you said how three generals suddenly entered your meeting. And then on page 24 of the transcript, you said, "When Mladic, Gvero and Tolimir came to Zvornik." The Prosecutor asked you when they came, and you said, I'm not sure. I think it was a month or more before Srebrenica. Based on all that I've said, my question is: Because you've said this into the transcript, it turns out that perhaps you didn't know. Can you please tell me, did this happen before the Srebrenica events? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it before or after the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I cannot really say definitely. I said I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said -- you said this, I quote: "I'm not sure. I think that this was one month before Srebrenica." That is what you said. All I'm saying is that you said that you are not sure. Are you sure that this was before the Srebrenica event? You're not sure -- you're not sure about the time. Was it before the events or after the events? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Well, let's say that I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether this was, then, after the Srebrenica events? Are you able to recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it during the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: No, it was not during the Srebrenica events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it before or after the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I told you I was trying to check back. After the Srebrenica events was the Storm operation, the fall of the Krajina. We had meetings of the War Presidency then. I said that possibly, then, it could have happened before. This is the reason why I said that this happened probably before, because such meetings were not held after -- until after Srebrenica and until after a state of war was declared in Republika Srpska. But let's leave it at my saying that I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The answers that you gave to the Prosecutor, you say -- you

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What I meant to say at the closed session is this: that we need to redact the answer of the witness where he says what post he was carrying out at that particular time. This is all I meant to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be done. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, sir, the Prosecutor asked you, on page 14, whether the gentleman who received you at the office during that meeting at the brigade seat expected you to help him with the burials. He asked him [as interpreted] if he expected that, and you said, No, that was my conclusion. My question is: Do you stand by what you said, that this was your conclusion and that the word that the Prosecutor used was actually not used? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: You must admit that it's been a long time since then for a person to remember the details that are significant, yes, but I said that that is how I understood it. And judging by the turn of events later, there is some overlap there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I wanted to ask you. This is my conclusion on the basis of events that were discussed over and over again later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Should I answer something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I don't want to repeat it. I'm going to repeat it briefly. When you testified just now, did you state here, No, that is my conclusion? When the Prosecutor asked you if he expected you to help, did you say, as I wrote down, No, that is my conclusion? Just say yes or no. Thank you. Not four years ago, but did you say it now?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I would need to read it back. I mean, this is an English text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the general issuing an order to the witness to answer yes or no. That is inappropriate. And the general has an effect on people, and orders should not be followed like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see it as an order issued to the witness. He's asking for a short answer, like he did in the last months already several times. It's another question if it's always appropriate to force a witness to give short answers, especially for this witness who is providing the questioning party with quite short answers. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps my conclusion was unfair. What I'm objecting to is his raised voice and when he said, "Just say yes or no." I think that's inappropriate. I think that's an unfair way to influence a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a question of the voice. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as the tone is concerned, Mr. Tolimir has a very powerful voice, but in no event is he using an imperative tone towards the witness or wishes to cause any kind of difficulty or to be unpleasant. Throughout the whole time he's doing his best to behave in a mild and an exemplary manner towards each and every witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, in most cases, also the understanding of the Chamber. On the other hand, we can observe sometimes that Mr. Tolimir is raising his voice a lot, and this can influence and put some pressure on a witness. Everybody should be aware of that. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for this warning. I understand the witness is unable to answer precisely because he does not have the transcript in the Serbian language before him. So I would just like us to look at page 11, lines 14 onwards, to see what the witness said. And I do take his request into account regarding the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question would be: Mr. McCloskey, on line 15 -- on page 15, line 3, actually, asked whether in the Popovic case you had seen on television that somebody had been brought to The Hague, and that it was said on television that the identity of this person was Mr. Beara, and that you said that this was not the same person that you had seen in the office during the Srebrenica events. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So on the basis of that, my question would be: Do you still stand by what you said, that you don't remember the face of the person you saw on television that was arrested as being the same person who was in the office? Do you stand by the statement that you gave in the Popovic case? That would be sufficient of an answer.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by what I said in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 10, line 19, you said that Beara said that he was the barracks commander; is that correct? Did I understand you correctly? Did I quote you correctly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: He said something to that effect, that he was in charge, that at that moment he was in charge there, that his word was to be listened to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the barracks?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there's a problem with the interpretation. Do you receive everything in your language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At one point, I didn't hear Mr. Tolimir in my headphones, but like this. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement, from page 8 to 10, the investigators put questions to you. Can we look at P1356. Can we see that on the screen, it will be easier to follow. And I don't want to mention the name of the person, but you told the person that is in line 5 -- I don't want to identify that person because that might identify you, but you will see that person's face on the monitor now. Thank you. If possible, can we look at P1356, please, page 10. I don't want to say the name, so that the witness would not be identified on the basis of those names. So let the witness read. This is page 12 in the English. Aleksandar, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document is under seal and should not be broadcast. And if there are portions to discuss about, we should consider the possibility of going into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I can use the name without the document, but then they are going to discover the identity of the witness by the name. I don't want to do this. I can use the name without going into private session, but then I will disclose, with the help of that name, the identity of the witness. Perhaps the witness can look at the statement and it doesn't have to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will not be broadcast, and we wait for the moment that it is coming up on the screen. And everybody knows then what is in that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to look at page 10 in the Serbian. Page 10 in the Serbian and page 12 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, line 5, there is a first and last name there. In line 8, we have his position. The same is in the English version, for the Chamber. My question is this: Since you know who this person is and you know what his position was, I wanted to ask you whether it would have been logical, in terms of your position, to contact this person under the prevailing circumstances at the time. Yes or no, thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes. And I had frequent contact with him, as a matter of fact, more than with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it the duty of the municipal organs to provide for the municipal unit that was in its territory, as was requested of you by the person who was in attendance at that meeting when myself and General Mladic arrived?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I don't remember anything of the sort being prescribed by the law, but I believe we saw it as our main task, to assist the soldiers of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase the question. Providing food, clothing, and everything that was necessary for the soldiers in that area, was it something that was supposed to come from you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Well, they had to receive that from the army, but the army did not have such resources, and we took it upon ourselves to provide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Under such circumstances, did you not have to pay such funds into the army accounts instead of providing supplies?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Well, yes, that would be the ideal situation. But during the war, there was no revenue and no taxes collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This obligation that was upon the municipal authorities, was it something that you had to do, given the fact that you were not assisting the military budget in financial terms?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone. You need your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 17 of the statement in the Serbian, please. Thank you. In the English, Aleksandar, it is number 20. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Without mentioning any place names, so as to protect your identity, please read line 27 and 28, following which I will have a question for you. Indicate to me, please, when you are done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which line is it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 20, it should be the same line. In the Serbian, it is line 27 and line 28, and my assistant will tell you exactly what lines those are in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English, it is page 21, line 3, and we are using the statement as a means to protect the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In line 3, you used the word "krece," "coming." Based on what you said, was that group moving in marching order or in combat formation?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: They moved in combat formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this why you expressed your concern for your family and the inhabitants, because of the sheer amount of people who had arms moving about?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: At that time, the people in the town were really afraid because all of the able-bodied men were at the front-lines. The town, itself, was not protected. I think in the statement, itself, I mentioned that we asked the army to send Mr. Pandurevic and his unit back to Zvornik to protect us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you, but it is time for our first break. We will have the first break now and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to say that in the last answer of the witness a name was mentioned which may be used to identify the witness. Perhaps we should redact that. It should be left in the transcript, but that part should not be made public. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your position, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If they're referring to the -- I see no problem with that. That's a historical event. It's the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. It's very well known. It doesn't tend to identify him in any way, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's also my position that there is no reason to redact that part. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe your judgement will be better than mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your concern. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 18, line 33, in the Serbian, and page 22, lines 18 to 21, in the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are still using the document P1356, which should not be broadcast; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am using it so that I don't have to read out loud anything that may identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have a look at the last sentence. I'm interested in the end of that sentence, where you say that the army was above civilian authorities. My question is this: Was the VRS a municipal or a republican entity?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: The military was a republican entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did anyone from the army -- or was anyone from the army under an obligation to report on the activities of the military to the municipality or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: They were under no such obligation. However, occasionally there were situational reports at municipal meetings; not necessarily at the level of the republic but in the municipality, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said in the statement that the army was above civilian authorities, did you have in mind only the civilian authorities in your municipality or in the entire republic?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact background, the context, but we know that in democratic societies, the military is always below or under the control of civilian authorities. And at that time, we lived in a democratic society.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we go to page 19 in the Serbian, line 14 as well as line 15, and in the English, page 23, line 4. Thank you. We can read this out loud. I will do so, skipping a single word which may identify you: "After the fall or liberation of Srebrenica, did you hear about the Muslim population being taken in the direction of" your area? I will not refer to the name mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Can you tell us whether the Muslim population referred to by the investigator were being taken to the area or were they, themselves, trying to break through, passing through your territory and near a town that was not protected, given the fact that all of the able-bodied men were at the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Those of them who moved in combat formation were not being taken anywhere by anyone. They were going by themselves to Tuzla and that area. They were not being taken anywhere. They moved in combat formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the fear of the population justified in such circumstances? Because, as you say, there were only a dozen people who had not been mobilised. Were such fears of the population realistic if there was a large number of people crossing their territory who were armed and were basically the enemy at the time?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes, people were very afraid because it was a narrow strip alongside the Drina River from Srebrenica to Tuzla. At any point in time there existed a possibility that they should turn on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes. There was much fear among the population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we next have page 20 in e-court, lines 20 and onwards. In the English version, it is page 24, lines 28 to 30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On this page and the next, which is page 21, when the investigators took your statement, asked you about the participation of your father-in-law in the transport of Muslim prisoners, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you provided answers, you said that you were worried because he did not come back from the task he had assigned to him by his company. You also said that for a while he was in a state of shock, because he was on a bus full of Muslim prisoners who were guarded by soldiers of the VRS, because at some point in time they managed to seize those weapons from the soldiers and train them on those guarding them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Later on in the statement, you say that at some point fire was opened on the bus where your father-in-law was, which contributed further to his nervous breakdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get precise references? Because I'm reading very different -- a very different substance of what the general is repeating, and I'm not sure where he's talking, but in the pages that he's talking about, there's two different incidents of shooting going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have that part on the screen at the moment. Are you referring to a portion on page 25 of the document in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I'm referring to page 24 in the English, lines 28 to 30, where the witness describes how his father-in-law drove a bus full of Muslims, which is in line 29, Mr. McCloskey. Page 24, line 29, and as well as lines 32 and 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your last question -- it was not a question yet. In the beginning of your last question, you said, I quote: "You said that at some point fire was opened on the bus where your father-in-law was, which contributed further to his nervous breakdown." I can't see anything like that in this part of the OTP statement we have on the screen now. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's on page 25. And the witness gave a very specific reason for that, and it doesn't have anything to do with what the general is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would like to have that on the screen now, the next page. Mr. Tolimir, are you -- can you tell us from which part of this page you are quoting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am quoting from page 20, lines 25 to 33. I am now going to quote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 24 in the English, lines 28 to 30. Actually, 28 to -- 26. Thank you, Aleksandar. I'm only going to quote sentence 32 and 33, which is going to answer, then, the question that the Prosecution has and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says, 33: "You mean Muslim men or women and children? "A. I am thinking of men and only two -- only two policemen or soldiers, some, and they seized the weapons from soldiers and policemen." This is page 25 in the English, the first few lines, where the witness is talking about how his father-in-law was driving a full bus that was guarded only by two soldiers, and their arms were seized. That is what it says in line 33. They grabbed the weapons from soldiers or police officers. And then later on page 25, as Mr. McCloskey said, he's explaining something, and he says on page 21, line 13 - that is, the following page of the English - where it says, in line 13, Serbian version 21/13: "And he died a year and a half ago from a stroke."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, in fact, in the English version, page 25, lines 16 to 19 or 20. And now your question, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's leaving out lines 14 through 18 -- 14 through 17, which, in my reading of this, are the most significant parts of the psychological damage to his father-in-law, from this interview. So he can't ask that question unless he fairly puts it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I can read those lines: "I know why he told me lots of times, and this left a mark on him. I think that he had consequences from the stroke." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the basis of this, my question was: Were there any shots fired, in the bus that was driven by your father-in-law, by the people who had grabbed the guns from the two escorts that were in the bus? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: There were combat-able or able-bodied men, Muslims, in the bus, and they were guarded by two soldiers or policemen. The Muslims grabbed the weapons from those two escorts and fired inside the bus. A panic broke out, and then the other soldiers or policemen that were outside fired at the bus, and my father-in-law was not able to get out because he didn't have a door. There was no door next to the driver. So this brought on this shock, and that's why he had to retire. But, basically, there was fire from both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for clarifying this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we please scroll down the English version to enable us to see lines 21, 22, 23, to the bottom, please. To the bottom, please, that's all. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, we are slightly confused by the lines. Now we have the French translation -- now we have the French translation on the English channel. I don't know what happened. You were talking about lines 31 to 33. Where are these lines? We are lost at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any line 33. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The page I was referring to was on page 25. I thought he was referring to 25. This is where the story of the Muslims getting the guns and shooting people is. And we don't have page 25 up on the screen in English. I don't know what page we have, because lines 14 through 17, like I said, on page 25 have another story that appears different from or related to what General Tolimir is saying. But I don't -- I think he's talking about page 25, and that's not what's on the screen right now in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't know what page it is on the screen at the moment. I think 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: I think it's 25, should be 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the end of 25 is line 32. There is no line 33. Could you clarify, for the Chamber and the Prosecution, what you are quoting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor to look at page 20 in the Serbian version, lines 24 to 33, in the Serbian. In the English, that is page 24, lines 28 to 26 [as interpreted]. And on the basis of that, I put the question to the witness, and the witness answered, and he can repeat the answer, and from the answer, it will be clear who fired at his father-in-law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat the number of the lines again. It was interpreted "lines 28 to 26," and that can't be correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that that is what General Tolimir said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the English, can you look at lines 24 to 30. Thank you. Page 24. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is on the screen now. Thank you. And now put the question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I put the question to which the witness has already given his answer before we got into this confusing situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who fired at the bus in which the Muslims were being transported, and how many armed people were guarding the bus, and how did it happen that the arms -- weapons changed arms? Could you please answer the Trial Chamber? That was my question. I mean, you answered it a little bit earlier, but I need to repeat it because of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: The bus was being guarded by two soldiers or policemen of the Army of Republika Srpska, with weapons. At one point, the captured Muslims grabbed the weapons from those two soldiers and started shooting inside the bus, at the soldiers inside the bus. A panic broke out, and then the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska who were outside started to shoot at the bus, the part of the bus where these soldiers with the weapons were. My father-in-law was sitting in the driver's seat. He was not able to leave the bus because there was no door next to the driver, and that is when his medical problems began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. All I wanted to do was to clarify who was firing, because this was not correct in the statement, and now you have explained that. Thank you for your answer. The point of my question was to clarify what was unclear in the statement, because it was just said "soldiers," but there was no clarification as to whose soldiers they were. Thank you. Can we now look at page 24 in the e-court. This is page 24 in the Serbian language. This is line 24 onwards. And that is page 29 in the English. Can we see the page we asked for, page 24, lines that we asked for from 24, so that the witness can see this page. I'm going to read or quote from line 24. These are lines 14 and 15 in the English, where it says: "At the same time, the army in the field, there were 3.000 prisoners," meaning that he had to kill 3.000 prisoners, bury them. That was a huge logistical problem. And then line 27 -- this is all spoken by the investigator: "Can you tell me how the municipality helped in the clearing and burial of all those bodies?" Based on that, my question is: While you were being interviewed by the investigator, is that the first time that you learned of this figure of 3.000 soldiers and about this information that allegedly the commander of your brigade from your municipality sent to his superior, the corps commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, because I was just focusing on the reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, the investigator, quoted to you a part of the statement that the commander of your brigade from your town sent to his superior commander at the corps, and he said there what I quoted. He mentioned 3.000 soldiers, and he said -- he said that they had a problem, that they needed to kill the citizens and then bury them. I quoted that, and what I asked was: Was it -- the first time that you heard about this figure, was that from the investigator, and was that the basis for his continued questioning you as if you had said that?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: No. The investigator read to me the dispatch that the brigade commander sent to his superior with this content, and I think I answered that I was not familiar with exactly what happened in that situation. And it's evident that these are the words of the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted you, for the transcript, to tell us whether it was that first time that you heard this number from the investigator and these terms that he used that relate to that number of 3.000.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you. That was the first time that I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. My next question is: Did you have the sense during the interview that the investigator, Nicholls, tried to get you to say things that he already had in the documents that were sent by your commander or from other reports or other interviews with other persons? Was he trying to get you to say these things that were already contained in other documents?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I already answered that I was in a terrible mental state at that point in time when I was led to answer these questions, which I was not prepared to answer when I arrived for the interview, because I was convinced that I could avoid answering the questions on this particular topic. I don't know if the Prosecutor or the inspector led me to answer. I really, at that point, couldn't tell. I couldn't sense anything like that. I wasn't in a stable state in order to be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you, as you said, immediately after the meeting that you talked about, went to the coast, at that time were you aware at all of what was happening in the municipality? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: I didn't know anything until I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And this statement of yours, was it drafted on the basis of information that you could have acquired later, after you came back from the coast? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Well, it's a fact that I learned about it all later, not at the time that it was going on, not immediately, but later, even years later, because this was a topic that was frequently discussed also in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this information that you found out second-hand, through stories, or did you find out about it directly by virtue of your function and the job that you were doing?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: This topic was not discussed at any meeting. More information was gained from conversations and from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you came back from your holiday, did you have any superiors in your structure, municipal structure, who were more responsible than you for the whole situation that happened during the events, themselves, and after the events, in view of the fact that a state of war was declared? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Later, when the state of war was declared, the president of the War Presidency was there, but at no point in time -- we never put the events on the agenda, what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, for the transcript, whether you, during the time that you were on holiday -- and if you can perhaps tell us how long you were on holiday, if you can give us the date, during the time you were on holiday, did you receive any information about the activities in the municipality that were happening in relation to the circumstances that you were interviewed about by the investigator? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: No, I did not have any contact with anyone, and I didn't know what was going on. There were no mobile phones around at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, for the record, when you returned from the seaside? Can you recall the date in July or was it perhaps already in August?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: In late July. I can't recall the exact date, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have all the events been resolved in the area of your municipality concerning the column that was trying to break through that territory, the Muslim column?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes. I think that column, in combat formation, went on to Tuzla. There were many, many casualties on both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for testifying, and thank you for providing answers to the best of your recollection. Please forgive me if at any time I have raised my voice. It was not my intention, but this is my nature and the way I speak. I would like to thank the Chamber and all those who assisted us during this examination. I would like to thank the Presiding Judge for his understanding. Mr. President, as far as my cross-examination goes, I am through with the questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I was not under the impression that you were ordering me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a small amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said there were lots of casualties on both sides when that Muslim column went through the area. Are you aware of any Muslims in that column that were picked up and buried by the Serb municipal authorities or any Serb organisation?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: No. The rumour that existed at the time was that the Muslims took all of their casualties with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was the fighting done -- as far as you know, were there minefields all around where a lot of that fighting went on, near Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes. I think even today there are still minefields in the territory of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you hear at the time or at any time that anyone from Zvornik went into those -- across those front-lines into the minefields to retrieve Muslim dead?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: No, I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to the section in your interview. I have it as page 21 in the B/C/S. It should be P1356, and page 25 in the English, and it's -- we can see this -- the part -- if you could take a look at, I think, lines 10, 11, 12, 13 in the B/C/S, but in the English I see it on line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, before that, you tell the story that your father-in-law is driving a bus when the Muslims took some weapons and shot some Serbs, but then you go on, on line 16, and you say: "Then, he was in civilian clothes. That's when they took out all of the people to kill them, and he was with them, he was amongst them. They didn't know that he was different. Somebody recognised him and managed to save him. He died one year and a half ago from a brain stroke." What is that that he's telling you? What is he -- what is he telling you about, that they took all of the people to kill them?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: He told me that once the incident was over, that everyone was taken off the bus and that they were ready to kill them all, and that he was among them since he was in civilian clothes. Apparently, someone recognised him and pulled him out. But he didn't tell me that all those people were, indeed, killed or anything of the sort, so I have no information whether they were later on killed, because I didn't put many questions to him. He would always tell me that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did he tell you that they -- the Serbs, the Serb forces, like you say here, took -- and I quote, "took out all the people to kill them"?

utterances.speaker: PW-065
utterances.text: Yes, they emptied the bus, with him being with the others. I don't know whether they killed them, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you will be happy to hear that this concludes your examination. You are now free to return to your normal life and normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and for the answers you were able to provide. Thank you again. And we turn into closed session for a moment to enable the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session, Your Honours, once the blinds are shut.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Now we are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everyone. You may be aware that we had a witness that was on last Thursday, I think, and we're prepared to proceed with the redirect examination. It should be fairly -- it should be fairly brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were referring to the witness Tomasz Blaszczyk?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I'm actually referring to the witness Erin Gallagher, and I was informed she was actually testifying earlier this week. I'm mistaken, but Monday it was, okay, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was because of --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If that's the reason for the confusion, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the holiday on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there is nothing to raise, the witness should be brought in. In the meantime, I would like to ask the Prosecution if we have received a list of exhibits to be used with Mr. Blaszczyk and to be added to the 65 ter exhibit list. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I was with Mr. Thayer as he and Ms. Stewart were getting that list together, and, yes, it's basically the list -- I think it was the list used in the other case. As I mentioned, many of the documents did not have a 65 ter number, as yet, because we hadn't gotten that far, but that's why you may see no 65 ter numbers. Ms. Stewart is going to be working on that. I think some might, and she can, of course, assign others so it can be up-loaded in e-court properly. But that's something we had spoken to Mr. Gajic about, so he's aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem for the Chamber is we would like to know about the content of the testimony and the list of exhibits to be used with the witness before we grant leave to add him for this purpose to the 65 ter witness list and all the documents, so that we can proceed in the normal way like with all other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. And Mr. Thayer was getting that list together, he was at the photocopy machine, and we can provide those to you any way you like. But they should be -- I'm not sure how they are electronically, but they are going to be, I think, downloaded into e-court as the next step, and so that's now proceeding, I believe, in the absence of Ms. Stewart. Her staff is doing that, and so that should be going on while we're doing this. Mr. Thayer is well aware of that, and he was racing around in that because he knows exactly what you said on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The only reason I ask is that we would like to be prepared before the witness is called tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I understand that, Your Honour, and, of course, I know the Bench's feelings on that, and I know the Bench's feelings from Judge Schomburg before you on that, and so I've learned that that is something that is expected in this Chamber. And we are getting those things as soon as we can. I'm sorry it's come this late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are referring to a former Judge of this Tribunal. I understand what you are talking about, but I'm talking about this Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I apologise. What I mean is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understood you, Mr. McCloskey. No worries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand the culture where the Judges get everything. It's so counter to other cultures, but I have understood that culture and have lived with it and worked with it for many years, so I understand absolutely. I know it sometimes it doesn't appear that I do, but I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No worries about that. Sorry, Ms. Gallagher, for this discussion in your presence. Welcome back to the courtroom, and I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Vanderpuye has some more questions for you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll need 65 ter 2183 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Ms. Gallagher.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know that I only have a few questions, or, I should say, a few issues to redirect you on. On page 7758 of your testimony on 15 November, you were asked a number of questions by General Tolimir, one of which was -- concerned, I should say, the DNA samples, whether or not it would be more appropriate to receive DNA samples from closer relatives rather than more distant relatives, and you may recall that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the witness answers: This is confidential, as I was told, and it should not be broadcast. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There are parts of it that I think should not be broadcast. This part is all right, and I'll refer to a page -- we'll go to page 12, which should also be okay to broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Gallagher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall that series of questions that you were asked?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, in particular, you were asked at that page in -- General Tolimir put to you the following question. He said -- and this is page 7758, I believe it starts at line 1. He said: "Thank you for your answer. I asked you why distant relatives would give DNA samples and why this would be taken as more valid information than DNA samples taken from closer relatives." And he referred to the following example. He said: "My following question has to do with Witness PW-14 for whom you said it was the boy who was called by his father. You said that he was only identified in the Krstic trial in 2004.
